description_full: Collegium Pharmaceutical, Inc., a specialty pharmaceutical company, engages in the development and commercialization of medicines for pain management. The company's portfolio includes Jornay PM, a central nervous system stimulant prescription medicine that contains methylphenidate HCl for the treatment of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder; Belbuca, a buccal film that contains buprenorphine for severe and persistent pain that requires an extended treatment period; Xtampza ER, an abuse-deterrent, extended-release, oral formulation of oxycodone for the management of pain severe enough to require daily; Nucynta ER and Nucynta IR, which are extended-release and immediate-release oral formulations of tapentadol, indicated for the management of acute, severe, and persistent pain; and Symproic, an oral formulation of naldemedine for the treatment of opioid-induced constipation in adult patients with chronic non-cancer pain. Collegium Pharmaceutical, Inc. was formerly known as Collegium Pharmaceuticals, Inc. and changed its name to Collegium Pharmaceutical, Inc. in October 2003. The company was incorporated in 2002 and is headquartered in Stoughton, Massachusetts.

financial_summary: Collegium Pharmaceutical, Inc. is a small-cap healthcare business with a $787M market cap on $781M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +19% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +613.5pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 170% against a 8% cost of capital — a 162-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 58% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $328M in free cash flow — roughly 42 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 5.24× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 2.2× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 3.2% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.
